texts.text: is a hypertext system developed by Peter J. Brown at the University of Kent in 1982 and later commercialized by Office Workstations Ltd. Unlike most systems, it used a replacement-based link model where destination nodes expanded into current nodes, allowing hierarchical navigation. It was ported to multiple platforms, including Macintosh and Windows, and evolved from a word processor into a CD-ROM multimedia system. Ian Ritchie, OWL founder, later reflected on missing an opportunity to adapt Guide for the web. Brown won a technical innovation award in 1988 and passed away in 2007.

OWL gradually shifted the focus of Guide from a low-cost hypertext word processor to a more expensive
multimedia development system.
Unlike most hypertext systems, the main link mechanism in Guide is based on

, meaning that when following a link, the current node breaks open, making room for the destination node. The anchor of the link is replaced by the contents of the destination node, like an expanded node in an

, but without the restraint of a hierarchical outline. One can close the destination node, which means that it is once again replaced by the text of the anchor. Thus, the basic method of navigation using Guide was the expansion button, by which a section was replaced when selected and expansion provided additional levels of detail. This allowed the user, whether a document author or a reader, to expand and contract a document, viewing the desired level at any time, not unlike viewing methods used in
files. This method required a hierarchical document structure.
Guide supported pop-ups for small annotations, and jumps, which behaved like the follow-link operation in most hypertexts (as in van Dam's
system). The jumps allowed for the non-hierarchical link creation.

author.text: Huan Nguyen, Soumyakant Priyadarshan, ChenCheng Jiang, R. Sekar, Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages, Association for Computing Machinery (2026), pp. 1127-1151

texts.text: Binary code analysis is vital for software security and reverse engineering, but disassembly is often error-prone. Current methods require disassembly before analysis, but disassembly accuracy depends on static analysis, creating a loop. The paper introduces a new static analysis approach that works

disassembly by analyzing a super-set control-flow graph derived from all possible instruction offsets. This method avoids invalid code path pollution using backward analyses and achieves linear time efficiency (O(n)), drastically outperforming prior techniques.

text.text: Binary code analysis plays a central role in numerous applications in software security, performance optimization, reverse engineering, and so on. Existing techniques need to first disassemble binaries into functions in assembly code before an analysis can be performed. However, disassembly and function identification have proven to be major challenges for complex variable-length instruction sets such as the x86. A recent trend has been to use static analysis to improve the accuracy of these tasks. This raises a chicken-and-egg problem: a disassembly is needed for static analysis, but a static analysis is needed for accurate disassembly! We overcome this problem by developing a novel static analysis approach that can operate before committing to a disassembly. Our analysis operates on the output of exhaustive disassembly that considers each possible offset in a binary as an instruction, and constructs what is known as a super-set control-flow graph (CFG). The central technical challenge in analyzing this CFG is that it mixes legitimate instructions with unintended ones, causing analysis results from invalid code paths to pollute legitimate ones. To overcome this challenge, we begin with a key new insight that if we focus on backward analyses, we can ensure accuracy of analysis results at intended instructions even though we have no idea where these intended instructions are! Moreover, our analysis operates in time that is linear in the size of the binary. Specifically, in O(n) total time, it yields analysis results for every one of the n offsets in an n-byte binary. For this task, it is orders of magnitude faster than previous techniques, as the previous techniques typically need to repeat the analysis many times.

webpage.description:
Step inside the studio of Palestinian-American artist Samia Halaby, one of the earliest innovators of digital art.

In the mid-1980s, Halaby bought an Amiga computer and taught herself how to code. With it she produced bold, colourful 'kinetic paintings', consisting of vivid, brightly coloured geometric shapes and slanting lines shifting restlessly in all directions. For Halaby, these works were a continuation of the abstract paintings she had been creating in oils and acrylic since the 1960s.

In this film, we travel with Halaby from her New York studio to London for a special musical performance at Tate Modern, as well as the opening of a new commission at Outernet London, where her works are shown on a scale like never before.

See Halaby's work in Tate Modern's exhibition Electric Dreams: Art and Technology before the Internet, on until 1 June 2025: https://www.tate.org.uk/whats-on/tate-modern/electric-dreams

Research supported by Hyundai Tate Research Centre: Transnational in partnership with Hyundai Motor

webpage.author: Raymond Chen

text.text: In memory of the man who put red and green squiggles under words

texts.text: , a legendary but under-recognized Microsoft developer who worked on nearly every version of Word and ported

, is remembered for revolutionizing the spell-checking feature. He transformed spell-checking from a manual, blocking process into the familiar, real-time system that displays red and green squiggles under errors as users type, allowing for seamless editing without interruptions. His work, achieved by reverse-engineering the MS-DOS version for Windows, became the industry standard found in almost all modern word processors.

text.text: I recently learned of the passing of someone whose work nearly everybody knows, but nobody knows his name.

texts.text: Tony Krueger is
as the person who ported the game Chip’s Challenge to Windows for the Windows Entertainment Pack.¹ But that’s probably not the code he wrote that touched the most people.

text.text: Tony worked on Word 1.0, 1.1, 2.0, then on Word for OS/2 and Word for Mac, then returned to Word 6.0 and several versions beyond that. He probably holds the record for “most versions of Word shipped.”

In early versions of Word, the Spell Check feature was something that you explicitly invoked, and then you had to sit and wait while the program looked for all your potentially-misspelled words, and then showed them to you one at a time for a decision on what to do for each one. Word did introduce an Auto Spell Check feature to run spell check when the user was idle, so that when you hit the Spell Check button, the results were ready to go. However, the Auto Spell Check was still a blocking operation. As a result, a lot of users turned it off because it always seemed to decide “Now would be a good time to spell-check the document” just as you wanted to do something, forcing you to wait for the spell check pass to complete before you could, say, save and exit.

Tony made the spell checker much more unobtrusive so that it didn’t interfere with your foreground work. And when it found a problem, instead of waiting for you to trigger a spell check, it immediately drew red squiggles under potentially-misspelled words (and later green squiggles under potential grammatical errors).

Tony was an early fan of the magic/comedy team Penn and Teller. A friend and colleague attended a show and hung out afterward to ask the duo to sign a photo for his friend Tony. “He was on the team that did the red and green squiggles in Word.”

texts.text: Upon hearing this, Penn Jillette announced in his stentorian voice which filled the entire theater: “The red and green squiggles!? I
the red and green squiggles!” Teller silently concurred.

text.text: Tony received that autographed photo for his birthday, and it wasn’t clear which he was more happy about, the autographed photo or the fact that Penn and Teller loved his feature.

texts.text: Many years later, “Weird Al” Yankovic recorded a parody video titled
, in which the Word red squiggles make a brief appearance. That same friend got “Weird Al” to autograph the screen shot.

text.text: Today, there are red (and even green and blue) squiggles in nearly every word processor, and often outside word processors. Tony did it first. The next time a red squiggle catches one of your mistakes, say thanks to Tony. I think he’d appreciate it.
¹ Probably not as widely documented is that he accomplished this without the source code: He reverse-engineered the MS-DOS version and then reimplemented it for Windows.

📚 Conheça a Livraria Além do Fato! Uma seleção de livros sobre tecnologia, história, computação, ciência e temas que ajudam a ir além do óbvio.
👉 https://livraria.canalalemdofato.com.br 

Em plena ditadura militar, muito antes do Orkut ou do Facebook, o Brasil criou a sua própria "rede social". O Projeto Ciranda (e seu sucessor público, o Cirandão) conectou milhares de pessoas de forma pioneira, utilizando computadores nacionais de 8 bits e conexões telefônicas rudimentares. Neste vídeo, Mike Douglas revela a história oculta desse audacioso experimento da Embratel: a utopia de recriar as assembleias democráticas no ambiente digital, o nascimento do primeiro jornal eletrônico brasileiro e a guerra silenciosa de bastidores entre os protocolos estatais fechados e o padrão TCP/IP aberto, que acabou decidindo os rumos da nossa internet. Descubra como esse elo perdido da nossa informática formou a elite técnica que hoje sustenta a rede que você utiliza todos os dias.

https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCF1wLSmLwdnKmSwPBUvHwyg/join

https://www.canalalemdofato.com.br

Capítulos:

00:00 - Deixe seu LIKE e HYPE o vídeo!
01:18 - COMO FUNCIONAVA O PROJETO CIRANDA 
03:00 - O NASCIMENTO DO CIRANDÃO E A REDE RENPAC
05:40 - A GUERRA INVISÍVEL DOS PROTOCOLOS
08:20 - O LEGADO PERDIDO DA NOSSA PRIMEIRA REDE SOCIAL

Fontes Consultadas:
Benakouche, Tamara. "Redes técnicas/redes sociais: a pré-história da Internet no Brasil." Uma análise sociológica e histórica fundamental sobre a transição do Projeto Ciranda para o Cirandão, detalhando custos de acesso, estatísticas de adesão e as dinâmicas de uso do sistema.  

Podcast Primeiro Contato (B9). "A internet antes da internet." Trabalho documental em áudio que resgata depoimentos valiosos dos engenheiros, arquitetos e pioneiros do Projeto Ciranda da Embratel e do Videotexto paulista.  

Histórico da Conectividade Brasileira. "Os primórdios da Internet no Brasil." Um mergulho na transição das redes acadêmicas e comerciais brasileiras, registrando o embate de protocolos entre o X.400 adotado pela Embratel (STM-400) e a escolha universitária pelo TCP/IP rodando sobre a infraestrutura física da RENPAC.  

Revista Iberoamericana de Ciencia, Tecnología y Sociedad (CTS). "Sistemas Distribuídos e a Política de Informática no Brasil." Pesquisa acadêmica sobre como os conceitos de redes distribuídas de computadores foram trazidos à Embratel por engenheiros formados no final da década de 1970.  

Revista Micro Sistemas (Novembro de 1982). "Projeto Ciranda: A Primeira Comunidade Teleinformatizada do Brasil." Cobertura histórica do XV Congresso Nacional de Informática da SUCESU no Riocentro, preservando o discurso e os ideais democráticos originais apresentados no lançamento oficial do projeto.  

Aventuras na História. "Videotexto: a história do serviço visionário que antecedeu a internet." Reportagem detalhada que contextualiza o funcionamento do videotexto da Telesp, sua expansão pelas capitais do Brasil e a concorrência tecnológica com o Cirandão.  

Educação em Revista (SciELO). "Do Projeto Ciranda ao SDITE: A rede de formação docente do MEC." Estudo histórico sobre como o Ministério da Educação (MEC) utilizou microcomputadores nacionais Itautec I 7000 para implantar o primeiro sistema nacional de ensino a distância baseado na metodologia de rede colaborativa da Embratel.
